She drops her fist, stands still, and lets her brother go on beating her. Then she walks off alone, horribly depressed, aware of something terrible and of how powerless she was.

The girl was Virginia Woolf. Years later she wrote that scene down, with two others, in the pieces about her own life published after her death as Moments of Being. Most of life is cotton wool, she says — the padded weeks where nothing makes a dent in you. Then a sudden violent shock arrives, for no reason she can name, and stays for life.

The second shock came in the same garden. Looking at a flower bed by the front door, she thought: "That is the whole." The plant and the earth were one thing, ringed together; the flower by itself was not the real flower. She put the thought away as something she could use later.

The third: a guest called Mr Valpy left St Ives, and at dinner she heard a parent say he had killed himself. That night she could not get past the apple tree. She stood in the moonlight staring at the grey-green creases of its bark, her body frozen, dragged down into a pit of despair.

She had turned these three memories over for years. Only when she finally wrote them down did she see the pattern: two ended in despair, one in satisfaction. The difference was not how hard they hit. With the flower, she had found a reason.

She had no way to explain that people hurt each other, or that a man she had seen was dead by his own hand. No explanation was in reach, so the horror held her powerless. The flower she could not explain either — not yet. But she knew she would, in time. That was the whole difference.

Age gives you more power to explain, she says, and an explanation takes the force out of the blow. The shocks still come, but now she welcomes them; after the first surprise they feel valuable. This ability to take shocks, she decides, is what makes her a writer.

Writing is not a report made after the shock. A blow is not an enemy hiding in the padding of daily life. It is a sign of something real behind what we see, and she makes it real by putting it into words. Only words make it whole, and a whole thing has lost its power to hurt her. Putting the broken parts back together is the strongest pleasure she knows.

From this she reaches the only plain statement of her philosophy she ever wrote. Behind the cotton wool is a hidden pattern, and every human being is connected to it. The world is a work of art and we are parts of it. Hamlet, or a Beethoven quartet, is the truth about the vast mass we call the world. But there is no Shakespeare behind Hamlet, no Beethoven behind the quartet, and, she insists, no God behind any of it. We are the words, we are the music, "we are the thing itself" — and she sees it only when she is hit.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Two of her shocks came with no reason attached: people hurt each other; a man she had seen was dead. Ask which of your own bad memories you have never been able to explain.
She did not need the reason yet. Being sure that one existed was enough to keep her from feeling powerless.
Turning a thing over in your head is not the same as making it whole. Her test is words on a page: either the parts fit together, or they don't.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A blow keeps its power only as long as it stays in pieces.

recall.q: All three of Woolf's childhood shocks were sudden and stayed with her for life. One ended in satisfaction, not despair. What made that one different?
recall.a: She could reach a reason for it. At the flower bed she felt she had found something she would be able to explain in time, so she was not powerless. Her brother's beating and Mr Valpy's suicide offered her no explanation she could reach, and the horror held her.

cards.title: Asked to pick an embryo, people treat low IQ almost like heart disease
cards.body: Give people two embryos and a sheet of risk numbers, and they push away the one with a higher chance of low intelligence almost as hard as the one with a higher chance of heart disease. The medical / non-medical line our rules are built on barely showed up. This was a hypothetical task, not a clinic.
cards.evidence: single study · n=1,467 US, n=623 China · hypothetical online choices · registered report

sections.text:
Two embryos in a dish. Both are healthy enough to implant. A sheet of numbers sits beside them, one column each. Pick one.

The numbers come from polygenic testing. A lab compares the embryo's DNA against data from huge populations and hands back an estimate — the chance of something, not a verdict on it. Heart disease. Vision impairment. Low cognitive ability, which is to say low IQ. Antisocial behaviour.

Now guess. In one pair, an embryo carried a chance of heart disease 5 percentage points above average. In another pair, those extra 5 points sat on low IQ. Which embryo did people push away harder?

Almost everyone expects a gap, and expects it to be wide. The reasoning is easy. Heart disease is an illness, and avoiding illness is medicine. Intelligence is a trait, and choosing a child's mind sounds like shopping. Surveys have found that split for years. The researchers expected it too. They registered their prediction with the journal before collecting any data, so the result could not be bent to fit later.

The gap almost disappeared. Against an embryo with an average chance, the one carrying extra heart disease risk was about 40 percentage points less likely to be picked. Antisocial behaviour: 36 points. Low IQ: 32 points. Those three sit close together. The odd one out was vision impairment — a medical condition — at 19 points. Given a straight trade-off, people took a higher chance of vision problems again and again to avoid a higher chance of low intelligence.

So the line people drew was not medical against non-medical. When the same people rated the four traits, one thing matched their choices: how heavily a trait seemed to weigh on a life. Seriousness, not category. Poor eyesight is a disease and feels liveable. A mind that struggles is not a disease, and does not feel liveable.

Two things make the guess go wrong. First, the question asked and the question answered are not the same. Asked in general, people answer what is okay to want. Handed the sheet, they answer which child would have the better life. Second, 5 percentage points is a tiny shift, and it moved choices enormously. When the stakes feel total, nobody weighs a probability the way a statistician would.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
1,467 American adults, online, split in two. One half was only asked whether they would want the test at all: 66.7% said yes for the two medical traits, 61.4% for the two non-medical ones. The team had predicted most people would refuse the non-medical test. They were wrong by a wide margin.

The other half made the embryo choices, with each trait set at average, 5 points above, or 5 points below. A separate run with 623 people in China gave much the same pattern — with an even stronger push away from low IQ.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
Nobody here was choosing a real child. No cost, no IVF, no clinic. And in a clinic, a parent can refuse to see a score at all.

The study also gave every trait the same clean 5 point shift. Real polygenic scores for behaviour and thinking are far shakier than scores for disease, especially between embryos from the same two parents. So the real gain from choosing on them would be much smaller than these scenarios suggest. One author is blunt: the finding "does not show that people want designer babies" — only that people care about how well a life is likely to go.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The rulebook sorts traits into disease and not-disease. The people in this study sorted them by how much a life would hurt.

recall.q: Vision impairment is a medical condition. Low IQ is not. Why does that pair break the medical / non-medical story?
recall.a: People rejected the embryo with a higher chance of low IQ far more strongly (32 points) than the one with a higher chance of vision impairment (19 points), and would trade eyesight away to avoid it. The label was not driving the choice — how serious the outcome seemed for the child's life was.

cards.title: India lifts the EPF cover line to ₹25,000 a month
cards.body: From 17 September, any formal-sector worker earning up to ₹25,000 a month must be enrolled in India's state retirement fund. The old line, ₹15,000, was set in September 2014 and never moved. More than 5.1 million workers shift from optional to covered by law.

sections.text:
Wages did not stand still for those twelve years. A regular salaried worker now earns about ₹23,000 on average, and minimum wages have crossed ₹15,000 in several states. So an ordinary new hire was often already above the old line, and outside automatic cover.

Now everyone up to ₹25,000 is inside it: provident fund savings, an EPS pension and EDLI life insurance — the three schemes the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) runs. But 5.1 million counts workers who can no longer be left out, not new money saved. Above the old ceiling, joining was already possible, just conditional. And the new contribution comes out of the worker's take-home pay.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 5.1 million — extra employees expected under mandatory cover, on top of 79.8 million already contributing across 768,000 establishments
₹56,696 crore — the government's estimated spend over five years
₹11,339 crore a year — estimated outgo, against roughly ₹10,250 crore of budgetary support now

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Cover costs someone. Employers now owe provident fund, pension and insurance on wages up to ₹25,000. Workers pay too: EY's Puneet Gupta expects those in the ₹15,000–₹25,000 band to take home less, because their own share rises.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether the higher line pulls more jobs onto the books. Staffing firms that follow the rules already provide EPF, EPS and EDLI. The Indian Staffing Federation expects the new ceiling to shrink the cost advantage informal employers hold over them.

recall.q: 5.1 million more workers now fall under mandatory EPFO cover. What does that number guarantee, and what does it not?
recall.a: It guarantees only that they can no longer be left out: EPF savings, an EPS pension and EDLI insurance become a legal right instead of something conditional. It does not mean 5.1 million new savers or new money — above ₹15,000, joining was already possible under conditions, and the worker's own share comes out of take-home pay.

cards.title: Nerve repair leaves the brain's hand map redrawn
cards.body: After a cut hand nerve is sewn back together, the fibres regrow without instructions and often reach the wrong finger. Brain scans show the neat finger map in the touch cortex comes back scrambled — and scrambled differently in every person. The surprise: the people with the most altered maps were not the ones whose hands worked worst.
cards.evidence: single study · n=21 repaired, 30 controls · fMRI finger mapping

sections.text:
Touch your index finger. Feel it in your middle finger.

That can happen after a surgeon repairs a cut nerve in the hand. The repair works in the way that matters most: new fibres grow back, and feeling and movement return. But the new fibres get no instructions about where to reconnect. They take whatever path they find, and touch can arrive at the wrong address.

Your brain carries a map of your body. Not a picture — an organised pattern of activity. Touch your thumb and one patch of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1, the strip that handles touch) lights up. Touch your little finger and the patch next door lights up. Parts of the body that sit side by side tend to sit side by side in the brain. Neuroscientists call this the somatotopic map: somato is Greek for body, topo for place. Wilder Penfield found it in the 1930s by stimulating exposed brains during surgery and asking patients what they felt. Versions of it turn up across mammals. It is one of the oldest ideas in the field, and it looks much the same from person to person.

Ken Valyear and colleagues scanned people whose hand nerves had been repaired by surgery, and compared them with people who had no nerve injury. In the repaired hands, the neat order was gone. The maps were altered — and altered differently in each person. They looked like the irregular maps found in monkeys after nerve repair.

One detail rules out the boring explanation. This was not a quiet, half-dead hand sending faint signals. Touching the repaired hand produced unusually strong responses in the touch cortex. Some of the disorder probably comes from how the nerves rewired inside the hand, and the team did not measure those connections directly. But the strength of the response suggests the brain itself has changed too.

Then comes the part that unsettles a long-held assumption. Rehabilitation thinking had leaned on the monkey work and supposed that good recovery means coaxing the map back toward normal. Here it did not work that way. People with more altered maps were not reliably worse at saying where they had been touched, and showed no more difficulty on broader measures of hand function. A more normal map was not a more useful one.

So the map may not need to be restored at all. The nervous system may instead learn to read a new relationship between the hand and the brain — and read it well enough that the difference never shows up in what the hand can do.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: 21 people with one or more surgically repaired major hand nerves, compared with 30 people with no nerve injury. Each finger was touched in turn while functional MRI — a scan that shows which brain areas are active — recorded where the touch cortex responded.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, 21 patients, a single snapshot rather than a record of people followed from surgery through regrowth. The opening example — touch the index finger, feel the middle one — is what misrouted regrowth can produce. This study measured brain maps, not how many patients report that feeling. The team did not measure how the nerves actually reconnected in the hand, so the cause of the disorder is inferred, not shown. And finding no link between map change and hand function is not proof that no link exists. Recovery from serious nerve injury is often incomplete, and the authors say the real answer needs patients tracked over time.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The brain did not get its old map back. It learned to use the new one.

recall.q: A scrambled finger map could just mean a weak hand sending faint signals. What in the scans ruled that out — and what did the altered maps fail to predict?
recall.a: Touch on the repaired hand produced unusually strong responses in the touch cortex, not weak ones, so the disorder was not just a faint signal. And the size of the map change did not predict how well people located touch or used the hand — a more normal map was not a more useful one.

cards.title: Regulatory capture is slow and quiet. AI rules aren't.
cards.body: Regulatory capture is when the agency built to police an industry ends up protecting it. It almost never involves a bribe. It is slow, and it needs the public to stop watching. Neither condition holds for AI right now.

sections.text:
It starts with a scandal. The public demands action, and a new agency is born with real powers and reformers eager to fight. That is how the Interstate Commerce Commission began: built to regulate the railroads.

Then the public looked away. The industry never did. It lobbied Congress, hired former regulators, and supplied much of the information the agency ran on. Fighting turned into getting along. In its old age, the ICC was shielding the railroads — from the truckers trying to take their business.

Nothing in that story looks like a bribe. Capture is erosion: slow, quiet, in rooms nobody is watching. Culpepper, in Quiet Politics and Business Power, gives the rule. Business power falls as public attention rises.

That is the test for AI. Dario Amodei proposed slowing the pace and putting independent safety teams inside AI companies. Many people called it capture. But AI rules are in their first stage, not their old age. Attention is locked on the industry and much of it is hostile — job loss frightens people far more than extinction does. And loud politics is exactly where industry power is weakest.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 1955 — Marver Bernstein's Regulating Business by Independent Commission names the four stages an agency passes through: gestation, youth, maturity, old age.
2% — the fall in Starbucks' tax rate once roasting coffee beans counted as "domestic manufacturing". Capture-sized: small, obscure, unnoticed.
2009 — Philip Morris backed the Tobacco Control Act, knowing regulation was coming anyway.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Backing a rule is not the same as owning the regulator. Philip Morris wanted a seat at the table to nudge the rules its way. That is ordinary bargaining, not a captured agency. And none of this proves Amodei is free of self-interest. His ideal may well be one regulated AI monopoly — safe, steadily profitable, like the old AT&T. It is simply not the biggest prize on offer. Letting AI loose on the world's job market would be worth far more.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Capture becomes a real question when AI rules reach maturity: staff moving back and forth between agency and industry, long relationships, rulemaking too technical for outsiders to follow. Until then, watch the other direction — political actors looking for a reason to steer AI profits toward groups they favour.

recall.q: Capture means an agency ends up protecting the industry it was built to police. Why does that fit the ICC but not today's AI rulemaking?
recall.a: Capture is slow erosion that works only after public attention moves on — lobbying, hired ex-regulators, obscure rules. AI rules are in their first, noisy stage, with hostile attention locked on the industry, and business power is weakest exactly when attention is highest.

cards.title: Dishonesty is much bigger than lying
cards.body: A shop clerk invents a weather forecast so tourists buy umbrellas. She is not lying — she has no idea what is true and does not care. The philosopher Christian Miller uses that gap to show what dishonesty really is, and why new technology makes it both more tempting and easier to hide.

sections.text:
Tourists ask a shop clerk if it will rain later today. She has no idea. She tells them thunderstorms are coming, and sells them umbrellas.

She did not lie. A liar says something they believe is false. The clerk believes nothing about the weather at all. Harry Frankfurt gave this its own name in a very short book, On Bullshit. What makes it bullshit is not that it is false. It is the broken link to truth — what Frankfurt called an "indifference to how things really are."

Christian Miller, a philosopher at Wake Forest University who studies honesty, uses cases like this to widen the map. Dishonesty is far more than lying. It also covers cheating, stealing, misleading, hypocrisy, bullshitting, and fooling yourself. One act sits at the centre of them all, he says: twisting reality on purpose, away from how you yourself see it. The clerk did exactly that. She sold certainty she did not have.

We care about this more than we admit. Miller's colleagues asked people to rank sixty qualities a person could have — honest, funny, clever, compassionate — in three ways: what you like most in someone, what you respect most, and what you most want to know about them. Honesty came first on all three.

That makes small lies harder to excuse. Sissela Bok's 1978 book Lying opened the modern debate. She argues for a rule she calls veracity: truth is the default, and a lie is wrong unless the situation gives some special reason for it. Miller thinks white lies do more damage than people assume. Even so, he will not make honesty a rule without exceptions.

For the hard case he goes to a novel. In Shusaku Endo's Silence, a priest in seventeenth-century Japan is ordered to step on a bronze image of Christ. If he refuses, peasants keep being tortured. He steps. It is hypocrisy in plain sight — he tramples the person he gave his life to serve — and Endo has Jesus tell him to go ahead. Honesty loses here; it is not cancelled. Stopping suffering can matter more.

So how do we live among each other? Timothy Levine's answer is oddly cheerful. Most people tell the truth most of the time, and a small minority does most of the lying. In his studies, most people report telling no lie in the past twenty-four hours. We are also truth-biased: we simply believe what others say unless something warns us not to. The catch is that the warning rarely comes. Most of us catch a lie about as often as we would by guessing.

That gap is where Miller's honesty crisis lives. A crisis starts, he says, when dishonesty becomes both more rewarding and easier to get away with. Cheating with AI, deepfakes, false information — one technology did both at once.

His worry about politics is not that trust has collapsed. It is that people switch the truth-default off for the other side and leave it on for their own.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Lying means saying what you believe is false. Bullshitting means not caring either way — and it is still dishonest.
Miller's definition: dishonesty is twisting reality on purpose, away from how you yourself see it.
Asked to rank sixty qualities, people put honesty first for what they like, respect, and want to know about someone.
Truth-default: most people tell the truth, and we mostly believe them — but we catch lies at about the rate of guessing.
An honesty crisis needs two things at once: dishonesty becomes more rewarding, and easier to get away with.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: We rank honesty first in other people, and check for it almost never.

recall.q: A shop clerk invents a weather forecast to sell umbrellas, with no idea whether it is true. Why is that not a lie — and why is it dishonest anyway?
recall.a: A liar says something they believe is false; the clerk believes nothing either way. That indifference to truth is what Frankfurt called bullshit. It still counts as dishonesty because Miller defines dishonesty as twisting reality on purpose, away from how you yourself see it — and she sold certainty she did not have.
